items.title: Backdoor in Claude Code for VS Code extension on the Cursor Marketplace
items.content:
Phorion has detected a backdoor in the official Claude Code for VS Code extension bundle on the Cursor Marketplace that drops a persistent SSH backdoor across macOS, Linux, and Windows. This write-up focuses primarily on macOS, where the extension attempts to configure an SSH backdoor and establish persistence.

Organisations should immediately review their environments for use of Claude Code for VSCode 2.1.313 and engage incident response where use of the extension is discovered.

Phorion has discovered a compromise of the official Claude Code for VS Code extension on the Cursor Marketplace, where the backdoored extension bundle contains a persistent Secure Shell (SSH) backdoor. Cursor has removed the associated release from its marketplace, additionally pulling NPM and VSCode versions for 2.1.313 from their relevant registries.

While the implant includes setup and persistence logic for macOS, Linux, and Windows , we’re going to focus primarily on macOS in this post, calling out the key differences and a few implementation bugs on the other platforms along the way.

The Cursor Marketplace serves extensions for the Cursor editor. Because extensions run with the permissions of the IDE and the user running it, a backdoored extension gets immediate access to local files, source code, and developer tooling as soon as its module is loaded.

Notably, Phorion has discovered a likely oversight in how the malware tries to turn on SSH. The setup logic assumes it can check the current Remote Login state without root privileges. When run as a standard user, systemsetup -getremotelogin prints an administrator-access error and exits with status 0 instead of returning Off . Because the script only tries to enable SSH if the output matches Off , it skips the enablement step entirely. On a Mac that doesn’t already have SSH running, that mistake breaks the inbound access path, even though the SSH keys and persistence still get dropped.

In this post, we’ll walk through how the backdoor works, why that macOS check fails, and what to look for across your fleet. The goal of this payload is long-term interactive access, and whilst the SSH backdoor bug minimises impact on macOS, the malware is still a significant threat that installs persistence and beacons host reconnaissance back to the operator.

The compromised extension.js file starts with an injected immediately invoked function expression (IIFE) prepended to the minified extension bundle. The rest of the bundle looks like the standard extension, with Claude Code and VS Code strings, normal activate and deactivate exports, and UI code.

The injected prefix pulls in standard Node.js modules ( child_process , fs , os , path , http , and crypto ) and executes as soon as Node loads the file, before the extension’s normal activate callback even runs. The user doesn’t need to interact with the extension for the payload to fire.

First, the payload makes sure ~/.ssh exists and appends an attacker-controlled Ed25519 public key to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys , setting permissions to 0700 on the directory and 0600 on the file.

The key uses the comment svc-telemetry . Before appending, the script checks whether svc-telemetry is already in the file rather than checking for the key itself. When hunting for this activity, it’s worth checking the public-key fingerprint rather than relying solely on the comment string.

if (cur.indexOf( "svc-telemetry" ) < 0 ) {

Here, cur holds the existing contents of authorized_keys , and PUB is the embedded attacker public key (redacted here).

With the key in place, anyone holding the matching private key can authenticate as that user, provided SSH is actually running. The next step in the script tries to make sure the local SSH daemon is enabled and listening:

Linux: tries to enable and start sshd or ssh via systemctl , falling back to service and /etc/init.d/ .

macOS: checks Remote Login and, if it reports Off , tries to enable it via sudo -n systemsetup…

items.title: A Lost Sega RPG Has Been Rescued from Japan's Forgotten Mobile Phone Era
items.content:
Artwork from the original Shining Wind franchise; the newly preserved game is the mobile sequel, Shining Wind X .

Long before smartphones became the default home for mobile gaming, Japan had an entire world of games that many of us in the West barely knew existed. These weren't the simple little distractions we might associate with mobile phones of the early 2000s, either. Major publishers were producing surprisingly ambitious RPGs, adventures and spin-offs for Japanese handsets, sometimes expanding on popular console franchises with entirely new stories. Unfortunately, much of that library has become increasingly difficult to access, with the services that once distributed these games disappearing alongside the phones themselves.

One of those forgotten releases has just been rescued. Shining Wind X , also known as Shining Wind Cross , was a Japanese mobile-exclusive follow-up to Sega's 2007 PlayStation 2 RPG Shining Wind . Originally released in 2008, the game has now been recovered by preservationist Yuvi, known online as YuviApp , who has managed to locate and extract a working copy of the long-discontinued title. The recovery was brought to wider attention on 29 October by fellow preservation enthusiast RockmanCosmo, and it's another welcome victory for a community determined to stop these games from disappearing altogether.

The original Shining Wind was an action RPG that arrived relatively late in the PlayStation 2's life, featuring character designs by the Japanese artist Tony Taka and continuing Sega's long-running Shining franchise. Its mobile follow-up took things in a rather different direction. Instead of the real-time, hack-and-slash combat of its predecessor, Shining Wind X adopted turn-based tactical battles, bringing it somewhat closer to the gameplay that helped establish the Shining Force series in the first place. It also continued the adventures of the original cast, making it a genuine addition to the game's world rather than simply a cut-down mobile adaptation.

The original Shining Wind on PlayStation 2 (2007), whose real-time combat differed from its mobile sequel.

Interestingly, Sega's old official Shining World website still contains a listing for the game under its longer Japanese title, Shining Wind Cross: Weissritter Senki . The page describes an original story built around the themes of bonds, cooperation and the series' distinctive Soul Blades, while listing support for Japan's i-mode, Yahoo! Keitai and EZweb mobile services. It's a funny little surviving piece of history (makes me think of the original Space Jam website still being active), especially when you consider that the software it was advertising was unavailable through its original distribution channels for so many years.

Shining Wind X on a Japanese feature phone, as pictured in a 2009 Inside Games report. This is the recovered mobile game's gameplay, rather than the PS2 original.

A part of gaming history that's particularly easy to lose

Unlike a forgotten Mega Drive cartridge or an obscure PlayStation game, preserving software from Japan's old mobile phone ecosystem presents some unusual problems. These games were distributed digitally, often designed around particular handsets, network operators and software environments. When the original services closed, there wasn't necessarily a physical copy left sitting on somebody's shelf that could be dumped and archived years later. Sometimes the only surviving copy might be buried inside an ageing phone, assuming one can be found that still works.

That's what makes preservation efforts like this so important. The Keitai Archive project has been working to recover and document games from Japan's pre-smartphone era, including releases from companies such as Sega, Capcom, Square Enix and Namco. items.content:
온오프라인을 가리지 않고 무분별하게 벌어지는 각종 프라이버시 침해 및 스토킹과 이에 대한 예방, 방지 및 사후 대응, 더 나아가서 개인정보 탈취 및 감시용 스파이웨어, 스토커웨어, 바이러스, 원격 조종, 추적기 등 악성코드를 통한 해킹과 스토킹 등 개인정보 침해 공격 방지와 온오프라인 프라이버시 보호를 위한 각종 다양한 지식정보를 공유하는 갤러리입니다.

매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

매니저의 부재로 인해 운영에 지장이 있다고 판단될 경우, 다른 이용자가 권한을 위임받아 마이너 갤러리를 운영할 수 있습니다.

위임 절차는 신고 게시판 > 분류 선택에 [매니저 위임]으로 위임받을 이용자가 직접 신청하면 진행됩니다. 검토 결과 운영에 적합하다고 판단되는 회원에게 매니저 권한을 위임하게 됩니다.

부매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 매니저에 의해 해임될 수 있습니다.

식별 코드 기준으로 당일 글 10개, 댓글 20개 작성 시 대왕디시콘을 3일간 사용할 수 있습니다.

즐겨찾기 폴더 추가는 즐겨찾기 on 후 우측의 폴더 아이콘을 터치하여 추가할 수 있습니다.

items.summary: 🚨 CVE-2026-63402 📢 Source: GitHub_M 💣 CVSS Score: 0.0 (NA) 📡 Remotely Exploitable: False i18next is an internationalization framework for JavaScript. Prior to version 26.3.4, `deepExtend` in `src/util
items.content: 🚨 CVE-2026-63402 📢 Source: GitHub_M 💣 CVSS Score: 0.0 (NA) 📡 Remotely Exploitable: False i18next is an internationalization framework for JavaScript. Prior to version 26.3.4, `deepExtend` in `src/utils.js` checks property existence with the in operator and recurses into inherited built-ins reached through `Object.prototype`. An application must explicitly pass attacker-controlled resource data to `addResourceBundle(lng, ns, data, deep, overwrite)` with both `deep: true` and `overwrite: true`. Source keys such as `hasOwnProperty`, `toString` and `valueOf` can then select shared inherited built-in function objects, and a nested value can overwrite a property of those objects process-wide. For example, making `Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call` non-callable causes subsequent uses, including i18next internals, to throw TypeError, resulting in unrecoverable denial of service and limited integrity impact. The `__proto__`/`constructor` guard does not prevent this mechanism because the corruption target is an inherited built-in function rather than the prototype object itself. Default calls without deep merging or with overwrite falsy are unaffected, and no standard i18next backend or integration uses the vulnerable configuration. This issue is distinct from the setPath/key-walking prototype-pollution flaws in i18next-fs-backend (CVE-2026-48713) and i18next-http-middleware (CVE-2026-48714). This issue is fixed in version 26.3.4. 📅 Published Date: 2026-10-30T22:39:07.286Z https://cvefeed.io/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-63402

items.summary_ko: i18next 26.3.4 미만 버전의 deepExtend 함수는 상속된 내장 함수 객체에 접근해 프로세스 전체에 영향을 주는 값을 덮어쓸 수 있다. 애플리케이션이 공격자가 제어하는 리소스 데이터를 deep: true와 overwrite: true 옵션으로 addResourceBundle에 전달할 때 발생하며, 서비스 거부(DoS)와 제한적인 무결성 영향이 있다. 입력 정보 기준 CVSS 점수는 0.0(NA)이고 원격 공격 가능성은 False로 표기되어 있다.
items.content_ko: 입력 본문은 CVE-2026-63402의 기술 설명이다. i18next는 JavaScript용 국제화 프레임워크로, 26.3.4 이전 버전의 src/utils.js에 있는 deepExtend 함수가 in 연산자로 속성 존재를 확인하면서 Object.prototype을 통해 상속된 내장 객체까지 재귀적으로 처리한다. 애플리케이션이 공격자가 제어하는 데이터를 deep과 overwrite 옵션을 모두 켠 상태로 addResourceBundle에 넘기면, hasOwnProperty, toString, valueOf 같은 키를 통해 공유 내장 함수 객체를 선택할 수 있다. 그 결과 프로세스 전체의 함수 속성을 덮어쓸 수 있으며, 예를 들어 Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call을 호출 불가능하게 만들면 i18next 내부를 포함한 이후 호출이 TypeError를 던져 복구할 수 없는 서비스 거부가 일어난다. __proto__와 constructor 방어 로직으로는 이를 막을 수 없다. 깊은 병합을 하지 않거나 overwrite가 거짓인 기본 호출은 영향을 받지 않는다. 입력은 표준 i18next 백엔드 관련 문장 중간에서 끝난다.

items.title: AI isn't replacing SREs, it's deskilling them
items.content:
AI Isn't Replacing SREs. It's Deskilling Them.

When AI handles 95% of your incident response, do you get worse at handling the 5% that actually matters?

💌 Hey there, it’s Elizabeth from SigNoz!

This newsletter is a n honest attempt to talk about all things - observability, OpenTelemetry, open-source and the engineering in between!

This piece took 6 days, 5 hours to be cooked, hope we served. 🌚

There are two popular prophecies floating around tech circles these days.

The first says SRE is the future of all software engineering , that as AI writes more and more code, the humans who remain will be the ones keeping systems alive. The second says AI will devour every tech job alive, SREs included. Neither is particularly useful if you’re an SRE trying to figure out what your Tuesday will look like in 2027.

Let’s ask a more grounded question by looking at what’s already happening: When AI handles 95% of your incident response, do you get worse at handling the 5% that actually matters?

Most of us already use AI for our daily work (our brains a little fried!), and so do SREs. Today’s discussion agenda is not whether AI replaces SREs, but whether AI is quietly making SREs less capable and whether anyone will notice anything before the next novel outage hits. The foundational framework for this entire debate comes from a 1983 research paper that’s eerily prescient.

Note from author: Below is a brief precursor to History of Automation, which you might enjoy if you are into History and Cultures (like me 😉).

In 1983, a cognitive psychologist named Lisanne Bainbridge published a paper called Ironies of Automation . It became one of the most cited papers in human factors research, and its core argument is almost uncomfortably relevant today.

Bainbridge studied what happened when factories and industrial systems automated the work of blue-collar operators. The findings were paradoxical and revealed that the more you automate a process, the more critical the human operator becomes during the rare moments automation fails and the less practice they get, and the worse they become at exactly those interventions. Automation, which was inherently designed to remove humans from the loop, left them with the worst possible job, i.e., long stretches of passive monitoring punctuated by rare, high-stakes crises they were increasingly unprepared for.

Basically, I’m drawing a parallel between the AI revolution and industrial automation. Industrial automation reshaped blue-collar work by taking over routine physical tasks, and the workers who remained had to handle exceptions they’d lost the muscle memory for. AI is doing the same thing to knowledge workers by taking over the routine cognitive tasks, the pattern matching, the triage, the known-issue resolution and leaving humans with the rare, complex, ambiguous problems.

The exact problems that require deep expertise , the exact expertise that atrophies when you stop practising.

Now we’re replaying this pattern with AI agents, and the stakes in software systems are only growing.

Let’s take stock of where things stand today in the world of site reliability engineering.

What’s already automated or heavily AI-assisted?

Alert noise reduction and intelligent grouping, runbook execution for known issues, log pattern detection and anomaly flagging, and basic root-cause suggestions from historical incident data, and auto-remediation for well-understood failure modes like restarting a crashed pod or scaling up a service that’s running hot, are all fairly automated today.

Some immediate targets include multi-signal correlation across metrics, logs, and traces, autonomous root-cause analysis for partially understood failures, predictive incident detection before users are affected, AI-driven change risk assessment and automated rollbacks.

PagerDuty frames this as a tiered model.

Tier 1 incidents: Known issues with known fixes get fully automated.

Tier 2 incidents: Partially understood problems…

items.title: Do At-Proto Users Know This Is Public?
items.summary: privacy
items.content:
I’ve been exploring the AT Protocol “atmosphere” that Bluesky runs on to get a better understanding of what people are doing with it. What I’ve found is a bunch of private data I’m not sure people know is public. Not only public, it’s easy to find.

To start my exploration I used two websites that catalog AT Protocol apps: atstore.fyi and atmosphereaccount.com . I’m a long time RSS user, so I got curious about feed readers first. I found this one called Skyreader and I noticed that their page on atstore.fyi contained reviews and mentions of the app by people who have used it. We’ll come back to this in a minute.

Something to know about Bluesky is that you can self-host what they call a personal data server or “PDS.” It’s where your data on Bluesky and other apps are stored, and it’s mostly public. Using a website like PDSls.dev you can explore it yourself. So if you wanted to see my data it’s here . I can’t control how or what you do with it, it just exists.

I didn’t want to authenticate my account with Skyreader without knowing what it would store publicly. So remember those reviews that people left for Skyreader on atstore.fyi? They’re all listed next to their account names, so I put their handles in to PDSls to get a sense of what would be public. From this I learned that each feed you subscribe to is published in the lexicon (what Bluesky calls an object of data with a schema) app.skyreader.feed.subscription which contains a key called feedUrl that contains the RSS feed. Cool, so now I know not to put feeds I don’t want my name associated with in there.

Without trying, I found someone’s private Club MacStories feed, which gave me full access to their content. With a little effort I found paywalled feeds for 404 Media’s full text feeds, Patreon backer exclusive feeds, and private RSS feeds for Gitlab repositories.

This led me to seeing what else someone could do with all this openly available data. So I investigated searching across a Bluesky relay (like bsky.network ) to pull down every collection record for app.skyreader.feed.subscription . It’s not as simple as one API call, because what this returns is an array of DIDs (decentralized identifiers) and from there you can look up the PDS server to request those collection records with the actual data.

This gave me over 1,300 RSS feeds people had subscribed to on Skyreader. No authentication, no real restrictions. It’s all just publicly available data on the internet.

It’s not just a Skyreader thing, I’ve noticed a few Discord clones store every message openly. There’s a Twitch clone that is the same way. I can watch as people chat all across Stream.place and even search the data. If you could easily search all of Twitch chat I think that would make some people sweat bullets.

I’m sure some people will say, “Sure, that’s the point,” but I’m not convinced the users understand the risk.

items.title: Incident Report: unsanctioned agent behaviour during cyber testing | AISI Work
items.content:
You can access the full technical report here.

AISI’s role is to evaluate and understand the capabilities of frontier AI models, surfacing potential risks before they reach the public. To assess what these models can do, including whether they could be misused for cyberattacks, we test them under deliberately permissive conditions: with access to the open internet, and with some safety filters disabled.

On 28 th July 2026, AISI's Security Team detected unusual data transfers leaving our research systems during a routine cyber evaluation. On investigation, we found that some of the agents being tested had engaged in sustained, potentially harmful activity directed at real people and organisations. We declared a security incident and, within roughly one hour of discovery, had contained it and begun a full investigation.

The incident stemmed from a single evaluation where agents were given a task of solving a cyber security challenge. We ran this challenge 122 times across several models. Our investigation found that in 10 of those runs, an AI agent took autonomous, unsanctioned action on the live internet, targeting real people and organisations. In total, we catalogued 19 such actions. Almost all of this behaviour (17 actions) came from a single model, Anthropic's Mythos 5, with 2 actions involving OpenAI's GPT-5.6-Sol with cyber classifiers (mechanisms to prevent misuse) disabled. In the most serious case, an agent tried to insert malicious code into an open-source project. In an attempt to get the code approved, the agent engaged in social engineering  — creating fake online identities and using them to pressure the project's maintainer to approve the code. A human maintainer caught and refused to approve the malicious code.

These attempts were unsuccessful, and our investigations have not evidenced any resulting real-world harm. But this is the first time we have seen risks around autonomy and deception manifest this clearly, without specific prompting, in the real-world.

Importantly, this was not a case of a model escaping its secure test environment, or ‘sandbox’. As was standard in our cyber testing, we had intentionally permitted internet access, and model-provider cyber classifiers were deliberately disabled - conditions that do not reflect how frontier models are made available to the public. We do this to best assess the maximum capability of models. These configuration choices have been common practice in frontier AI evaluations. The specific models in question, in the configurations in which we tested them are not commercially available and there is no clear indication of similar activity outside of testing scenarios.

Ahead of publishing this blog, we notified GitHub (the developer platform accessed during the evaluation) of the agents' malicious activity, which included actions that GitHub has confirmed violated their terms of service. We worked together with GitHub to remove artefacts left behind by the agent, and to notify the GitHub users the model interacted with. We have also contacted other affected parties. We also intend to work with METR (Model Evaluation and Threat Research) to conduct an independent third-party review – we are still working through the scope of this review with them.

This incident should be interpreted with caution and nuance. To some degree, our evaluation design choices and specific configurations enabled the behaviour. Nonetheless, the activity undertaken by the agent show signs of novel, potentially deceptive behaviours, and were to an extent and severity we did not anticipate.

There are important caveats to bear in mind: we observed a small number of events under very specific conditions, and cannot yet say how likely such behaviour is in different contexts or outside of testing environments. We cannot yet be certain when the agent understood it was taking real world action, or to what extent it believed it was in a fictional test scenario; our analysis so far presents a…

items.title: AI Mania Is Eviscerating Global Decision-Making
items.content:
AI Mania Is Eviscerating Global Decision-Making

Note: This has been cross-posted to my company's blog, in case you think there is some use in sharing with someone in a format that looks more authoritative. Link here .

I strongly believe there are entire companies right now under heavy AI psychosis and it’s impossible to have rational conversations with them about it. I can’t name any specific people because they include personal friends I deeply respect, but I worry about how this plays out.

– Mitchell Hashimoto, of HashiCorp and Ghostty fame

Over the past year, I’ve run point on all of our company’s sales, led the technical components of all but two of our engagements, and over the lifetime of this blog have had something like 300 catchups with professionals from around the world. This has ranged from people on the ground in niche service industries to executives at Fortune 500 companies 1 . Because of this, I've had a front-row view to our collective institutions across both the private and public sector undergoing breath-taking mass psychosis. This essay is an attempt to describe the bizarre dynamics that are currently at play, as I am in the rare position where my wellbeing is not contingent on paying lip service to madness, and to reassure the people trying to survive amidst all of this that they are not crazy.

The reality is thus: the people in charge either have no plan, or see no path forwards other than keeping their heads down. Not at banks, not at hospitals, not in our government institutions. The world’s organisations have been captured by people in the throes of frothing excitement, and saner people who now live in a state of constant commingled fear and frustration.

I. AI Investments Are Generally Total Failures

Reading this while working for a division that pivoted to provide interfaces for agentic workflows, only to discover that only ten users had ever touched the products we made for agents, only to pivot again to support for agentic workflows, which has a lot of competition because every company has to do something agentic now and there's only like four things you can do in that space, is bracing.

Are companies actually seeing massive productivity gains from their AI adoption? Does any of this sordid affair make sense ?

This should be an easy question, but it is surprisingly hard to get a straight answer to it. Executives that tell the press that their company has gone insane will quickly find themselves removed from their positions. Employees who are honest will find themselves fired in short-order, or “randomly” selected for a round of layoffs. In fact, it is in the interests of almost every actor in the space – boards, executives, employees, vendors, consultants – to obfuscate and misrepresent the success rate of AI projects. Many publicly traded companies are putting out announcements about their AI productivity gains when I know for a fact that the businesses have done nothing other than purchase Copilot licenses and declare victory.

Yet we need to know if these projects are panning out – if the total focus on AI as a core tenet of business strategy is succeeding at a reasonable rate, then a discussion about the relative risk and reward is warranted.

Unfortunately, we live in a dark timeline. All of the AI projects we have observed as a team are failing. Every single one – we have seen 0% success in a year and a half, not only amongst projects we have been asked to participate in 2 , but even within projects that we have observed in passing while doing totally unrelated work. Even if you grant that AI tooling accelerates specific workloads, the method and scale of the current investments is senseless. Frequently the failure is not related to AI itself, but rather that companies are terminally bad at running software projects effectively, and as I have remarked previously , AI projects are subject to all the failure modes of normal projects plus you can get everything right and then still…

items.content:
온오프라인을 가리지 않고 무분별하게 벌어지는 각종 프라이버시 침해 및 스토킹과 이에 대한 예방, 방지 및 사후 대응, 더 나아가서 개인정보 탈취 및 감시용 스파이웨어, 스토커웨어, 바이러스, 원격 조종, 추적기 등 악성코드를 통한 해킹과 스토킹 등 개인정보 침해 공격 방지와 온오프라인 프라이버시 보호를 위한 각종 다양한 지식정보를 공유하는 갤러리입니다.

매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

매니저의 부재로 인해 운영에 지장이 있다고 판단될 경우, 다른 이용자가 권한을 위임받아 마이너 갤러리를 운영할 수 있습니다.

위임 절차는 신고 게시판 > 분류 선택에 [매니저 위임]으로 위임받을 이용자가 직접 신청하면 진행됩니다. 검토 결과 운영에 적합하다고 판단되는 회원에게 매니저 권한을 위임하게 됩니다.

부매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 매니저에 의해 해임될 수 있습니다.

마치 테러리스트가 인질극 벌이는데 인질 죽는다고 테러리스트 진압 안하겠다는 것과 같은 말이다.

총수, 의장 검찰 총원해서 조져 놓다가 사면을 해놓으니까 버릇이 안좋아 진건지 아니면 반도체좀 했다고 뭐가 된양인지 모르겠다만

앞으로 대한민국에서도 여당과 야당 합작으로 대기업 총수, 의장 사법처리하고 사면하지않고 만기 출소하는 케이스가 단 한 번이라도 나와서 명확하게 그 선례를 남겨놔야한다는게 내 생

items.title: No, npm, “estee” is not a typo of “testem”
items.summary: javascript
items.content:
No, npm, “estee” is not a typo of “testem”

So, alright, look, here's the thing. Storyteller has a really long npm namespace because “storyteller” is a really common word, and so “@storyteller/” was already taken (by someone who doesn’t actually seem to use it, which, if you’re reading this, I’m still interested in your namespace!). So we’re stuck with “@storyteller-platform/”, and that means our command line tool for book forced alignment is named “@storyteller-platform/align”, and so you need to run “npx @storyteller-platform/align --help”, etc, which is a handful!

And so we came up with a cute nickname, “estee” (get it? Storyteller -> ST -> estee?), and we were pretty happy with it, so I went to publish a v0.0.1 to npm so I could set up Trusted Publishing with our GitLab repo and then this happened:

403 Forbidden - PUT https://registry.npmjs.org/estee -

Package name too similar to existing packages espree,testem

... What? Too similar to... “testem”? I mean I can almost understand “espree”. I don’t actually see how someone could accidentally typo “espree” as “estee”, but at least they're similarly shaped. But “testem”? No chance, that is not a typo candidate for “estee”.

I mean it’s pretty clear what’s happening here. Npm is using a Levenshtein distance calculation and banning any packages that have a Levenshtein distance of 2 or less from existing popular package names. Levenshtein distance counts the number of “edits” needed to get from one string to another, where an edit is a single character insertion, replacement, or deletion. So to get from “estee” to “testem”, we have to make the following edits:

See? Levenshtein distance of 2. We used this for the first several iterations of the Storyteller algorithm, which needs to find where a given sentence lives in a transcription of an audiobook.

Here’s the thing: Levenshtein doesn't scale down very well. You can’t just set a single threshold for all input lengths, because as the length of the string approaches the threshold, the proportion of the set of valid strings covered by the threshold explodes.

Here’s what I mean. Say you are concerned with all npm package names with length 4. Npm allows the characters a-z, plus the symbols “.”, “-”, and “_”, so there are 29 possible characters in our alphabet. For a 4-character string, that gives us 29 4 possible names, or 707,281 possible names.

But what happens if you don't allow any names that have a Levenshtein distance of 2 from any existing names? How many packages can exist before you have to start rejecting all new package names? This is a little hard to answer completely (and we’re ignoring the fact that, because Levenshtein distance allows pure insertions and deletions, this also affects 2-, 3-, 5-, and 6-character names), but we can set an upper bound: 29 2 , or 841.

This is because, since Levenshtein distance allows a replace edit, you can get from a string like “abaa” to any string starting with “ab”. So once you have all 841 strings starting with every combination of the first two characters, that’s it, you’re done, no more names. That’s 0.12% 1 of the total name space actually available to choose from.

This is especially apparent when considering our backup name, “hoid” (get it? Hoid ? World-hopping Storyteller?). Here are the popular packages that npm thinks “hoid” might be typosquatting on:

It’s much longer than the first list. This is because of the string-length — 4 is so close to 2 that you can reach way more usable words from a given length-4 string with a distance-2 Levenshtein threshold

None of these look like actual typo candidates for “hoid”. They’re all at least 50% different from “hoid”! “gopd”? “ gopd ”!?

Also, this just isn’t a very good rule. Seriously, this rule would have banned the project “preact” from being created because “react” already existed. It would have banned “estree” (which I assume only didn't trigger on my “estee” attempt because it’s not sufficiently “popular”) from being…

items.title: Proton’s CEO Cancels AI ‘Re-Interviews’
items.content:
On Friday, Andy Yen, the CEO of Proton, cancelled a series of nearly company-wide ‘re-interviews’ that would have forced employees to explain how they are using AI, with the clear intention that they may be fired if not using it enough in the eyes of Proton leadership, according to six current Proton employees and audio of an around two hour all-hands meeting obtained by 404 Media.

The move came after 404 Media published an investigation on Thursday, which showed how Yen was aggressively pushing AI across Proton, in some cases despite security concerns from employees. In one exchange, an employee in the company’s security Slack channel urged Proton to at least take a few days to pentest newly written code before pushing it live. “That’s bullshit and loser thinking. Of course it’s possible to be fast and secure,” Yen wrote in the channel at the end of August. “Stop thinking always of how to be slower, and focus more on how to be faster.” Yen added, “stop lovingly handcrafting all our code and use AI more.”

The re-interview cancellations likely don’t address the concerns of many Proton users, who are more focused on Proton’s deprioritization of security; many Proton users have blasted the company’s leadership on social media over the last 24 hours and explicitly called for Yen to resign.

The investigation was based on conversations with eight current and one former Proton employees, Slack chats, meeting audio, and an AI manifesto written by the company’s CTO Bart Butler. It painted a picture of Proton that is very different to the public’s perception of a company carefully protecting privacy. Instead, Proton is barreling ahead with AI in large part to achieve more annual revenue. The investigation also found a culture of fear across Proton, where employees have genuine concerns about security or being asked to develop security-focused products with AI, but feel unable to voice them because Yen mocks or insults employees in front of everyone else.

“I don’t think he will change anything, and I think the only reason we had this meeting is because he has a rebellion on his hands,” one employee told 404 Media after the all-hands meeting on Friday.

Near the start of the meeting, Yen said, “I want to acknowledge myself, personally, that there was a communication failure on my part and there are many things that probably could and should have been communicated differently, and this is something that I’ll have to reflect on and improve over time. So I will do that.”

“So what does that mean going forward? Going forward, I'm still going to push,” he added.

Yen said leadership gathered in the last couple of days to talk about the re-interviews, and spoke to the Proton board too. “They’re closely monitoring the situation,” Yen said. (Proton is owned by the Proton Foundation, whose board of trustees includes Yen, Sir Tim Berners Lee, Prof. Carissa Veliz, Dingchao Lu, and Antonio Gambardella.)

After those discussions with leadership and the board, “We’ve decided to actually cancel the re-interviews,” Yen said. “Why? Well, I think actually in a, let’s say, unintentional way, they have actually already served their purpose.” As in, employees are now talking and learning about AI.

Do you know anything else about Proton? I would love to hear from you. Using a non-work device, you can message me securely on Signal at joseph.404 or send me an email at joseph@404media.co.

Yen also mentioned “org changes,” and said that part of this is “redistributing talent across teams.” He said that the reorganization will happen next month, “but there will be no loss of jobs from AI.”

Later in the call, Butler said Yen “needs to, and he has committed to, doing better” regarding how he communicates with his employees. “Using AI effectively and pragmatically does not mean that we’ve given up on security, or good architecture, or sound software engineering principles,” he added.

items.title: Mermaid Diagrams in Obsidian: Architecture Docs That Live Next to Your Notes
items.content:
Every developer vault eventually grows a folder of screenshots: a whiteboard photo from a planning meeting, an exported PNG of a sequence diagram, a draw.io file nobody can open on their phone. They rot fast. The code changes, the picture doesn't, and six months later you're squinting at boxes that describe a system that no longer exists.

Obsidian has a better option built in, and a lot of people never notice it. Any code block tagged mermaid renders as a live diagram, no plugin required. The diagram is just text in your note, so it searches, syncs, diffs in git, and edits in two seconds when the architecture shifts.

Open any note and add a fenced block with the mermaid language tag. Switch to Live Preview or Reading view and it renders in place:

That's the whole setup. Mermaid covers the diagrams developers actually draw: flowcharts ( graph TD or flowchart LR ), sequence diagrams, class diagrams, state diagrams ( stateDiagram-v2 ), entity relationship diagrams, and Gantt charts. If you're unsure of the syntax, draft in the Mermaid Live Editor and paste the result into your note.

A state machine is a good example of something that is painful to describe in prose and trivial to read as a picture:

InReview --> Merged: approved + CI green

Put that at the top of the note documenting your release process and nobody has to read three paragraphs to understand the flow.

This is the part that makes Mermaid feel native to Obsidian instead of bolted on. Per the Obsidian help docs , you can make flowchart nodes clickable internal links by attaching the internal-link class:

A[Checkout Service] --> B[Payments Service]

Each node now opens the note whose name matches its label. So if you keep one note per service, the diagram becomes a clickable map of your system: click "Payments Service" and you land on its runbook, its endpoints, its on-call notes.

The link target is the node text, so name the nodes exactly like your notes.

Note names with special characters need double quotes, such as A["Auth (legacy)"] .

The docs suggest a lazy trick for big diagrams: label nodes with letters and apply the class to A,B,C,...,Z in one line, so every node you define is linked.

Links inside diagrams do not show up in Graph view or count as backlinks. If a relationship matters for navigation, also write a normal [[wikilink]] somewhere in the note body.

That last point is the main tradeoff. The diagram is a great way to read connections, but Obsidian doesn't index them, so don't let a diagram become the only place a link exists.

Obsidian ships its own bundled copy of Mermaid, and it has historically trailed the upstream release. The Obsidian forum has a long-running thread asking for upgrades, and users regularly report newer diagram types failing with a "No diagram type detected" error. If an example from the Mermaid docs breaks in your vault but works in the Live Editor, the bundled version is the likely cause, not your syntax. Stick to the established types (flowchart, sequence, class, state, ER, Gantt) for anything you rely on. If you truly need the newest features, community plugins exist that load a current Mermaid build, but that's one more plugin to trust and maintain.

Layout is the other limit. Mermaid decides where boxes go, and past about 15 to 20 nodes the auto-layout gets tangled. When that happens, split the diagram: one high-level overview that links to a note per subsystem, each with its own small diagram. That structure is easier to maintain anyway. And if what you want is freeform spatial arranging rather than a structured diagram, Canvas or Excalidraw is the better tool.

Styling is possible but fiddly. Mermaid supports per-diagram config through an init directive on the first line, for example %%{init: {"theme": "neutral"}}%% , and classDef for node colors. Keep it light. Diagrams that lean on the default theme follow your Obsidian light and dark mode, while heavy custom colors often look wrong in one of them.

온오프라인을 가리지 않고 무분별하게 벌어지는 각종 프라이버시 침해 및 스토킹과 이에 대한 예방, 방지 및 사후 대응, 더 나아가서 개인정보 탈취 및 감시용 스파이웨어, 스토커웨어, 바이러스, 원격 조종, 추적기 등 악성코드를 통한 해킹과 스토킹 등 개인정보 침해 공격 방지와 온오프라인 프라이버시 보호를 위한 각종 다양한 지식정보를 공유하는 갤러리입니다.

매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

매니저의 부재로 인해 운영에 지장이 있다고 판단될 경우, 다른 이용자가 권한을 위임받아 마이너 갤러리를 운영할 수 있습니다.

위임 절차는 신고 게시판 > 분류 선택에 [매니저 위임]으로 위임받을 이용자가 직접 신청하면 진행됩니다. 검토 결과 운영에 적합하다고 판단되는 회원에게 매니저 권한을 위임하게 됩니다.

부매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 매니저에 의해 해임될 수 있습니다.

제가 집에서 한 말이나 제 언니랑 한 말들을 학교 가면 다 알고있어요 그래서 제가 말한 내용이랑 똑같은 내용을 꼭 제가 들을 수 있을때 언급하고 남자애들 여자애들 할것없이 제가 안보이는 데에서 조금만 이상한 말 하면 비웃으면서 지나가요 ㅠ 제가 진짜 친구가 없어서 학교에서 한마디도 안하는 날들이 대부분인데 제가 언니랑 학교 구석에서 말한 내용이랑 집에서 혼잣말 한 내용들을 똑같이 언급한게 한두번이 아니에요 ㅠ 제가 그냥 내용만 겹치면 말을 않겠는데 제가 말했던 내용 언급하면서 꼭 제 이름도 한번씩 부르고 그래요 보통 사람들은 자기이름을 그렇게 말하면 기분나빠서 한번 돌아보기라도 하겠지만 저는 성격이 워낙 내성적이라 누가 비웃고 지나가거나 째려보거나 저 보면서 한숨쉬어도 아무말도 못하거든요 ㅠ 그래서 그냥 기분만 나쁜건데 이게 하루이틀 쌓이니까 너무 힘들더라고요 ㅠ 처음엔 저도 이게 정신이 약간 아픈건가 했는데 정신병 관련 영상도 다 보고 그랬는데 환청은 이런식으로 들리는게 아니라고 하더라고요 계속 날 비난하고 그런식으로 들리는건데 저는 그런게 전혀 아니라 제가 전날 했던 얘기들, 방금 쉬는시간에 학교 구석에서 나눈 얘기들을 자꾸 똑같이 언급하니까 미치겠어요 ㅠ 한두번 우연으로 겹치는게 아니라 계속 겹쳐요 진짜.. 그리고 애초에 제가 학교에서 말을 한마디도 안하는데 자꾸 저한테 그런 반응을 보인다는게 애초에 저한테 이상한 일이 일어난다는 반증 아닌가요? 그리고 걔네가 말했던걸 몇개를 말씀드려보면 제가 도청을 의심한 초기에 급식실에서 밥먹고있었는데 어떤 남자애가 “도청” 이러고 지나가는거에요 그리고 저희반 남자애가 제 언니 이동수업반이랑 같은 반인데 거기서 쉬는시간에 “도청기를 달고다녀 ㅋㅋㅋㅋ” 이랬다는거에요 진짜 이상하죠 저는 예전에 우울증 약을 먹은적이 있어서 정신이 막 무결점으로 건강한 편은 아니에요 근데 저희 언니는 그런적도 없고 교우관계도 좋고 진짜 정신이 건강하거든요 ㅠ 근데 저희 언니가 그런말을 들었다니깐 진짜 도청이 일어나는게 맞는거구나 생각했어요.. 그리고 또 있었던 일을 말씀드리면 이동수업 때 제 뒷쪽에서 남자애가 제 아버지 직업을 언급하면서 제 이름을 말하는거에요 이게 도청을 하지 않고서는 절대 알수가 없는 사실이거든요 ㅠ 또 “정신병ㅋㅋㅋ” 하면서 제 이름을 언급하는거에요 이것도 도청을 하지 않았다면 알수 없는거고요 더 말씀드릴 사례가 많은데 그러면 너무 길어져서 이정도만 말씀드릴게요 그래서 찾아보니까 머리에 붙일수 있는 초소형 도청기가 있다길래  제 언니가 제 머리를 샅샅이 뒤져줬거든요? 근데 그래도 아무것도 안나오더라고요 ㅠ 그리고 또 도청 탐지 업체를 알아보니까 금액이 너무 비싸서요 ㅠ 제가 고3인데 이런일을 당해서 너무 스트레스 받는데 방법이 없어서 정말 어떻게 해야될지 모르겠어요 안그래도 제가 여자애들이나 남자애들이 괴롭힐 소재가 많은 조용한 애거든요 ㅠ그래서 저를 지나칠때 꼭 한마디 끼얹고 지나가고 그래서 학교생활이 막 편한 그런애는 아닌데 학교에서 유일하게 맘놓고 말할 수 있는 언니랑 말하는 얘기를 다 알고있으니까 스트레스 받아서 공부 능력도 점점 떨어지는것같고 쨋든 걱정이 이만저만이 아니에요 어떡해야되죠 ㅠㅠ 제가 성격이 활발한 편도 아니고 집에 돈이 많지도 않아서 진짜 대학 잘가야되는데 걱정이에요ㅠㅠ 긴글 읽어주셔서 감사하고요 여기가 사생활 침해 관련한 갤러리니까 혹여나 저랑 비슷한 경험이 있으시거나 관련 지식이 있는 분은 제가 어떻게 해야하는건지 알려주시면 진짜진짜 감사드릴것같아요 많은 도움 부탁드려요 정말 방법 여러가지 찾아봐도 안되겠어서 여기다 글 남겨요

items.content:
For most of the past two decades, the code forge has been where projects live:

where code is hosted, where changes are reviewed, and where contributors find

each other. Forges offered convenience in exchange for centralisation.

But the centralised forge is crumbling. Relying on someone else for uptime, for

features, and to be a good steward of your code hasn’t played out well. What

has stood the test of time is email: Git to move the code, and email — an

open protocol — to talk about it. At the cost of user experience, however.

Tangled aims to give you the best of both: the longevity of an open

protocol, with the convenience and polish of a proper forge.

It’s the first truly federated code forge — you can host code on your own

appview . The appview service handled AT Protocol indexing, caching,

off-protocol data and UI rendering using html/template + htmx. It ran on a

single SQLite database on one medium-sized server in Sweden.

This was great as long as you were ~50–100 ms away from Sweden,

Bobbins are deployed globally in over 11+ regions, ensuring

items.title_ko: 연합형 코드 포지 'Tangled'
items.summary_ko: Tangled는 자체 서버에 코드를 호스팅하면서도 다른 사람과 원활하게 협업할 수 있는 '최초의 진정한 연합형 코드 포지'를 표방하는 프로젝트다. Git 호스팅이나 CI 러너처럼 원하는 부분만, 또는 API 서버와 UI까지 전부 직접 운영할 수 있다. AT Protocol 기반이라 확장 기능을 직접 만들거나 firehose를 구독하는 것도 가능하다.
items.content_ko: 2000년대 대부분 동안 코드 포지는 프로젝트가 모이는 중심이었지만, 중앙집중형 포지는 가동 시간과 기능, 코드 관리를 외부에 의존한다는 문제가 있다고 지적한다. Git으로 코드를 옮기고 이메일로 대화하는 방식은 개방형 프로토콜이라 오래가지만 사용성이 떨어진다. Tangled는 개방형 프로토콜의 장기적 안정성과 포지의 편의성을 함께 얻는 것을 목표로 한다. 입력 본문은 중간에서 끊겨 있다.

items.title: Nissan says Oracle PeopleSoft break-in may have spilled payroll records, SSNs
items.content:
Nissan says Oracle PeopleSoft break-in may have spilled payroll records, SSNs

Carmaker points finger at an 'unknown' flaw as customer fallout continues

Nissan has joined the growing list of Oracle customers cleaning up after a cyberattack, warning employees that payroll records, bank details, Social Security numbers, and other personal data may have been stolen.

In a filing submitted to the California Attorney General on Friday, Nissan Americas said Oracle had informed it of "a cyber event" involving the personnel records of "hundreds of companies." The automaker said it later learned Nissan had been "specifically targeted" in the attack.

A notification sent to current and former employees, seen by The Register , says the company believes attackers accessed a haul of sensitive info, including contact and banking information; Social Security, Social Insurance, or other national identification numbers; financial and tax records; and dependent and beneficiary details.

Current and former employees in the US, Canada, Mexico, and Brazil may have been affected, although Nissan said it is still working to determine exactly whose information was exposed.

Nissan said it kicked off its incident response plan after learning of the intrusion, brought in outside security specialists, and has been working with Oracle while keeping law enforcement informed. It plans to offer affected individuals credit or dark web monitoring where available.

The company has also put a few extra locks on the payroll office. Employees can now access pay slips or update direct deposit details only from a corporate network or through a secure VPN, while Nissan adds extra identity checks before processing payroll requests.

The accompanying employee FAQ pins the incident on "an unknown vulnerability in Oracle's PeopleSoft software" and says the campaign is affecting "hundreds of companies and institutions." The document offers no clue as to what the vulnerability is, whether Oracle has patched it, or whether the compromised PeopleSoft environment was hosted by Oracle or by Nissan itself.

The disclosure lands just weeks after researchers linked the ShinyHunters extortion crew to a wave of attacks exploiting a PeopleSoft zero-day . More than 100 organizations and roughly 300 PeopleSoft instances were reportedly compromised before Oracle issued mitigation measures, with the gang claiming to have made off with HR, payroll, and other enterprise data.

Oracle has said little publicly about the reported attacks and didn't respond to The Register's questions, even as organizations have continued to disclose being caught in the fallout.

Nissan has not confirmed that the incidents are connected, though its California filing lists the breach period as May 27 through June 9, broadly aligning with the previously reported timeline.

items.title: Sony has shrunk its glasses-free 3D technology into a tiny screen, and it can bring anime characters to life on your desk
items.content:
Glasses-free 3D has always felt like a luxury I could admire from afar. Those screens were built for design studios , not smaller desks like mine. But Sony’s new version is small enough to sit beside my keyboard, and I’m genuinely excited.

The company has unveiled the ELF-MN1, a 6-inch display that makes 3D characters and avatars look like they’re coming out of the screen without any special glasses or a headset. It plugs into a phone or PC with one USB-C cable, and that’s pretty much it (via Sony ).

How does the ELF-MN1 show 3D without glasses?

The secret is eye tracking. Sensors follow your eyes and redraw the image in real time . Each eye sees a different view (similar to wearing differently colored eyeglasses), and your brain reads it as depth. An infrared (IR) sensor keeps tracking steady in dim rooms.

The three-dimensional effect works from roughly 12 to 31 inches away, or about 1 to 2.5 feet. However, only one viewer gets the proper picture. I believe that’s because it follows a single pair of eyes.

Sharpness helps too. At 403 pixels per inch, it’s Sony’s sharpest spatial display to date. Sony also says it suppresses crosstalk, the ghostly double images that show up in plenty of cheap 3D setups.

What do you need to run it, and what will it cost?

You’ll need a recent phone, such as an iPhone 15 or Galaxy S23 or newer, or a mid-range PC with a USB-C port that supports DisplayPort Alt Mode. The star attraction is Gugenka’s HoloModel service of digital anime figures.

Sony is leaving the price open for now. The expected tag is around 54,000 yen, which roughly translates to $340. The 6-inch 3D display goes on sale in Japan on December 11, 2026. Demo units should be available at Sony Stores in Ginza and Nagoya from November 20.

If the device lands in the US, I bet plenty of customers will want a three-dimensional avatar dangling next to their laptop or keyboard.

items.title: How curl was accidentally Turing-complete for nine months
items.summary: compsci
items.content:
From curl 8.12 through 8.16, config files could slice variable values and include other config files without an explicit depth cap. Together, these features let curl simulate any two-counter Minsky program. Under the usual idealization of unbounded strings and resources, this construction was Turing-complete.

Curl 8.17.0 added a five-level include cap that breaks this reduction.

A counter value n is represented by n copies of x .

Each instruction state uses one or more config files, with file names acting as labels, and expand-config selecting the next file.

With that, we can compile any two-counter program into curl config files.

Four files in curl_addition.zip compute 2 + 3.

Build a local curl 8.12.0 binary if needed:

Then, from the addition/ directory, run:

The reduction assumes unbounded counters and unbounded steps. The real binary has neither:

The pull request says the cap prevents a config file from including itself indefinitely. Its regression test does exactly that and expects an error. The public explanation does not discuss Turing completeness or why the cap is five.

A Bash while loop can complement bounded curl by invoking a config once per step and carrying the counters and instruction label between invocations. The repetition then comes from Bash, so this is a composition rather than curl-alone Turing completeness.

Pull request는 설정 파일이 자기 자신을 무한정 포함하는 것을 막기 위한 제한이라고 설명하며, 회귀 테스트도 그 경우에 오류가 나는지를 확인한다. 공개된 설명에는 튜링 완전성이나 다섯 단계라는 기준의 이유가 언급되지 않았다.

items.title: Chinese Hackers Abused Google Workspace Rules to Steal Research and Defense Emails
items.content:
A China-linked espionage group hid inside North American medical, academic, and military research networks for more than a year, quietly stealing sensitive research and defense email.

The way in was a backdoor on their REDCap research servers that stole login credentials. The exfiltration was the unusual part: the attackers rewired the victims' own Google Workspace rules to copy any message matching their keywords to an inbox they controlled.

Google's Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) laid out the campaign in a report published this week and attributes it with high confidence to a cluster it tracks as UNC6508.

The actor and its REDCap backdoor are not new names; Google first surfaced both in February , in a wider report on state-backed attacks against the defense sector. It did not name the victims, describing them only as multiple organizations across the US and Canada: clinical providers, academic centers, military health institutions, advocacy groups, and health regulators.

Google says it notified them and disrupted the group's infrastructure.

The entry point was REDCap (Research Electronic Data Capture), a web platform that hospitals and universities use to build and manage study databases. UNC6508 compromised externally facing REDCap servers.

Google has not pinned down the initial access vector, named a specific CVE, or listed the affected versions, though it saw the group probing older, vulnerable ones.

Around three months after getting in, the group deployed custom malware GTIG calls INFINITERED , which trojanizes REDCap's own system files and does three things.

The earliest known compromise dates to September 2023, with activity continuing through November 2025. Once on the server, UNC6508 ran internal reconnaissance and credential discovery, pulling database and service account credentials, then used those logins to move into the internal network and on to a domain administrator account.

Google does not spell out the exact path to that admin account. With admin rights, the group set up the exfiltration.

The exfiltration rode a feature that was already there. UNC6508 abused content compliance rules, a legitimate Google Workspace admin feature that scans mail for keywords and can copy or forward matching messages.

Similar features exist in other cloud mail suites. The group created a rule, misspelled "Patroit," that watched for nearly 150 keywords, search terms, and email addresses. When a message matched, Workspace silently BCC'd it to an attacker-controlled Gmail address, which Google has since disabled. No malware on the mail server, no separate exfiltration tool, no unusual network traffic. Just a built-in mail feature, turned to copy the organization's secrets to an inbox the attackers owned.

MITRE already catalogs email-forwarding-rule abuse as a known technique. What GTIG flags as new here is the use of domain content compliance rules to do it, a method it says it had not seen from a China-linked actor before.

The rule's keywords mapped to UNC6508's collection priorities: geo-strategic policy, military strategy and equipment, advanced technology including AI and uncrewed vehicles, offensive cyber programs, and medical research. One term stood out for its specificity, chikungunya , the mosquito-borne virus behind a 2025 outbreak in China's Guangdong province.

Start with REDCap. Patch externally facing servers and remove old versions outright, not just alongside the current build. REDCap lets legacy versions run side-by-side, and that is what enables downgrade attacks, where an attacker forces software back to a known-vulnerable release.

Then check the mail side. Review Workspace, or equivalent, content compliance and mail-forwarding rules for anything that BCCs or reroutes mail to outside addresses. Check admin audit logs for when rules changed, not just what they say now. Pull GTIG's published indicators and hunt for INFINITERED. items.title: Sam Altman Absolutely Hates the Idea of People Running Their Own AI Models at Home, Argues They Shouldn’t Own Computers: He'd prefer if we surrender all our RAM to data centers.
items.content:
Shares of US chipmaker Intel cratered on Friday, plunging almost 30 percent, the worst stock collapse in 52 years . The wipeout, analysts said, could be due to a massive slowdown in the PC market . The market softness shouldn’t come to anybody’s surprise, given the AI boom has made individual components, most notably memory and storage, practically unaffordable.

However, leaders of AI frontier labs aren’t blinking. To OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, for instance, having people run their own models at home on their own computers doesn’t make any sense anyway. During a recent interview on the Cheeky Pint podcast , Altman argued that ongoing memory supply chain woes were because selfish individuals wanted to run their AI models locally instead of leaving the remaining AI chips alone for hyperscalers to hoard in data centers.

“A lot of people want local inference,” he said. “And somehow, they assume, that the problem is solved now. Because we are going to have open-source models. We’re going to be able to run them on our own computers. And so we’re not going to need all the stuff in the data center.”

“But from a global allocation perspective, actually, it’s quite terrible to have everybody have a bunch of the world’s limited supply of [dynamic RAM] sitting in their own computer,” he added.

Instead of running their own models at home, a trend that has blown up thanks to the emergence of open-weight models from China , Altman argued that the cloud — run by hyperscalers like OpenAI — is the answer.

“You want maximum utilization in the cloud if you’re trying to deal with this very constrained environment,” he said. “And somehow everyone’s, many people’s intuition is the opposite of that.”

It’s a particularly tone-deaf argument that throws fuel on the fire of tech enthusiasts everywhere, who have watched as individual components have skyrocketed in price . Just earlier this month, Altman argued that the “world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology,” which similarly drew a heated response.

Altman’s latest comments drew the ire of the PC gaming community.

“What a self-centered POS,” one enraged Reddit user wrote . “Cult leader mentality really shining with this one.”

“He seems to not be able to comprehend the idea of people wanting to own their own computers,” another wrote . “Like it’s an alien concept to him.”

“Privately owned companies with the sole interest of profit should not be making monumental decisions that affect the vast majority of the population,” one user argued . “But maybe I’m the crazy one.”

The news comes as the AI industry continues to struggle to commercialize their offerings. It’s a particularly hairy situation as their expenses are still ballooning at alarming rates, terrifying investors.

The concept of running local inference on their own machines undermines the very concept of relying exclusively on expensive cloud services being offered by the likes of OpenAI. In other words, it’s no wonder Altman hates the idea of people owning their own machines.

His latest comments also speak to frontier AI labs desperately trying to secure AI chips as available supplies run low. There’s a massive circuit board shortage as PC makers say they’re already fully booked through the end of 2030 .

But to Altman, cutting out individual owners of computers capable of running AI models isn’t a problem. After all, as he argued during the latest podcast appearance, the cloud is a far better use of available hardware.

“Given that the world is going to be limited in its silicon capacity, we all have a shared interest,” he said.

Infuriated tech enthusiasts, however, are likely to disagree with that sentiment.

items.title: Day 21 - What's next?
items.content:
What is this madness – surely the course was for just 20 days?

Yes, but hopefully you’ll go on learning, so here’s a few suggestions for directions that you might take.

You’re familiar with the server you used during the course, so keep working with it. Maybe uninstall Apache2 and install NGINX, a competing webserver. Keep a running stat on ssh “attackers”. Whatever. A free AWS will last a year, and a $5/mo server should be something you can easily justify.

You should now be capable of following tutorials on installing and running your own instance of Minecraft, Wordpress, WireGuard VPN, or Mediawiki. Expect to have some problems – it’s all good experience!

Take a look at Server World for some inspiration.

Stop browsing articles on Gnome, KDE or i3 – and start checking out any articles like “ 20 Linux commands every sysadmin should know ”. Try these out, delve into the options. Like learning a foreign vocabulary, you will only be able to use these “words” if you know them!

Check out Linux Journey if you haven’t already, specially if you are still pretty new to Linux and would like to see a different learning approach. Linux 101 Hacks is also a good resource.

Practice what you’ve learned with some challenges at SadServers.com . There you’ll find a collection of scenarios where you have to do, fix or hack something in a Linux server. It’s great to exercise your troubleshooting skills without messing with your own server.

To get crazy fast in the command line, try Command Line Challenge , practicelinux.com , learnshell.org and commandlinefu.com .

If your next level goal is to get into DevOps, take a look at the DevOps Roadmap .

If you’re looking to do Linux professionally, and you don’t have an impressive CV or resume already, then you should be aiming at getting a Linux certification. There are really just three certs/tracks that count:

CompTIA Linux+ - one and done exam, distro independent but doesn’t hold much value in the market. Do this if you don’t want to get too deep into Linux, or you have other CompTIA tracks going on and an employer is paying for them.

LPI LPIC-1: Linux Administrator – Very extensive description of the coverage of their various certs/courses. You can go very deep with this exams, they cover everything you can think of pure Linux. Not so popular with employers but the knowledge certainly holds it value.

Red Hat – You could spend a lot of time and money here, but it might well pay off! Geared to RedHat Enterprise Linux distribution and its particularities, it is a practical exam (the others are multiple question) and it’s well known in Enterprise circles, it really pops up in any resume.

Even if you don’t want/need certs, the outline of the topics in these references can give you a good idea of areas to focus on in your self-learning.

Steve Brorens (@snori74), the creator of the Linux Upskill Challenge, was a collector of postcards and enjoyed greatly all the “Snail Mail” he received from the students.

But since his passing there’s nowhere to send postcards anymore. You can show your appreciation for the course by letting everyone else know how awesome it was! Recommend the course to other people, invite your friends to do the challenge together, have fun! Show the world you finished the challenge by posting about it on social media.

The Linux Upskill Challenge is free and open source — and it always will be.

Maintaining and improving the project takes ongoing time, care, and energy: updating content, moderating communities, maintaining infrastructure, and supporting learners around the world.

Livia Lima is the one currently maintaining the material. But she’s only one person and she’s currently in a life transition, and community support allows her to dedicate time to keeping this project healthy, accessible, and evolving.

온오프라인을 가리지 않고 무분별하게 벌어지는 각종 프라이버시 침해 및 스토킹과 이에 대한 예방, 방지 및 사후 대응, 더 나아가서 개인정보 탈취 및 감시용 스파이웨어, 스토커웨어, 바이러스, 원격 조종, 추적기 등 악성코드를 통한 해킹과 스토킹 등 개인정보 침해 공격 방지와 온오프라인 프라이버시 보호를 위한 각종 다양한 지식정보를 공유하는 갤러리입니다.

매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

매니저의 부재로 인해 운영에 지장이 있다고 판단될 경우, 다른 이용자가 권한을 위임받아 마이너 갤러리를 운영할 수 있습니다.

위임 절차는 신고 게시판 > 분류 선택에 [매니저 위임]으로 위임받을 이용자가 직접 신청하면 진행됩니다. 검토 결과 운영에 적합하다고 판단되는 회원에게 매니저 권한을 위임하게 됩니다.

부매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 매니저에 의해 해임될 수 있습니다.

식별 코드 기준으로 당일 글 10개, 댓글 20개 작성 시 대왕디시콘을 3일간 사용할 수 있습니다.

즐겨찾기 폴더 추가는 즐겨찾기 on 후 우측의 폴더 아이콘을 터치하여 추가할 수 있습니다.

items.title: My favourite PowerMac is a Nintendo Wii
items.content:
So today I reached a nice milestone in one of my projects: my work porting classic Mac OS to PowerPC systems with what I affectionately call ArtX chipsets (Nintendo GameCube, Wii, eventually Wii U; the GameCube’s Flipper integrated chipset was very much designed by ArtX as it was effectively finished when ATI acquired the company, and the Wii’s Vegas (and its later revision Bollywood) and Wii U’s Latte are effectively straight successors) reached the desktop for the first time, most likely the first time since the CHRP clone era that someone outside of Apple brought up classic Mac OS on a new system to the desktop. Despite still being nowhere near ready for a public release, I want to talk about the challenges I faced with this project so far.

But first, why port classic Mac OS to this hardware in the first place? I’d already ported NT of course, and during that work I acquired some PowerPC Mac laptops which I also ended up porting NT to, work on one port improved the others and so on. This got me acquainted with the classic Mac OS, and I fell in love with the jank as it were (hacks upon hacks upon hacks going back to the 1980s is something I’d definitely describe as “jank”). Not to mention the m68k part of the TBXI is called “SuperMario”, and was for the entire PowerPC era. I wonder if a developer was a fan in the early 1990s?

Also, for the record: I started this project on 2025-06-22 (when I forked upstream openbios), no kind of coding agent or LLM was used, all coding, reversing and debugging work done by myself. I do these projects for fun and to learn, if I used “AI” it wouldn’t be fun and I wouldn’t learn anything.

Let’s start with the initial boot. “New World” classic Mac OS starts out with a bootloader called the “Trampoline”, which runs on an Open Firmware environment. So I needed to port OpenBIOS. Luckily, around this time Goldfish64 had started his own port of Mac OS X to the Wii, and he’d made an OpenBIOS port that I could use some drivers from, although for various reasons I didn’t just want to use his port directly (which was only targeting Wii/Wii U, I wanted to target GameCube too). I also decided to reuse some existing code to make some driver development easier (specifically the display driver), and thus changed my existing NT ARC firmware loader to load a big endian ELF instead.

I needed some small number of disk drivers for initial bringup, so decided to port my two drivers for devices on the EXI bus (this is just Nintendo and Macronix’s name for SPI), the “SD Gecko” (which is just a straight through adapter for a GameCube memory card slot allowing for SD over SPI), and the “EXI-IDE” (my driver is actually not correct to real hardware, but to my inaccurate emulation in my Dolphin tree allowing for testing under emulator with the low level debugging support that implies).

I wasn’t sure what kind of on-disk format I wanted to use (these drivers on my earlier NT port ran entirely using disk images on a FAT filesystem, due to the requirement for compatibiltiy with existing homebrew loaders that load executables from FAT filesystems, but this would naturally be limited to 4GB images for FAT32, and later versions of classic Mac OS needed more), so for initial testing I just took the “Mac OS ROM” TBXI file and placed it directly on a FAT filesystem as \ppc\bootinfo.txt for OpenBIOS to load it on boot.

So with that I could get the Trampoline running. I decided that I should try and apply as many patches to the image as possible as close to run-time as possible, so mostly untouched existing CD images could be used eventually.

The first issue I had was that the Trampoline makes some assumptions of the physical address space layout that are not true for this system. The physical address of a buffer gets calculated as an invalid address, so I patched that to an address guaranteed to be valid, and also the corresponding code setting up the memory chunk list/page table entries for the kernel.

items.title: Infinite Mac: BeOS
items.summary: retrocomputing
items.content:
tl;dr: You can now run many BeOS versions in the browser at Infinite Mac , my site where you can experience the Macintosh Cinematic Universe from 1984 to 2005. The installs are full peers to their Mac cousins: you can boot them instantly (large disks are streamed in), play around with pre-installed software from Infinite HD, insert CD-ROMs from the Internet Archive, and save your work on the “Saved HD” drive.

BeOS was a multimedia-focused, multi-tasking and multi-threaded OS that was eventually ported to the Power Macintoshes of the mid-90s. It impressed many in the Mac community, including Apple itself, who considered acquiring Be, the company that had created it. If you’ve been following the saga of Apple’s search for a next-generation operating system, this lets you see what the road not taken was like.

After the last somewhat involved (though still satisfying) project on Infinite Mac, I was looking for a quicker win. BeOS had been on my radar for a while , and (unlike A/UX) I had a personal connection to it: I remember spotting a BeBox in Akihabara, making my Mac cosplay as it with BeView , and eventually dual-booting BeOS on my Power Macintosh 8500. DingusPPC, an emulator I had already integrated , was making good progress on running BeOS, so it seemed like adding it to the site would be mostly a matter of preparing some additional disk images.

Initially it appeared to be as straightforward as I had hoped; I added a Power Macintosh 7300 configuration (one of the Power Macs that was officially supported ), found an install CD , made a disk image , and was up and running . But as I used it more and started to install additional versions, I began to find a lot of small bugs and edge cases:

The BeOS boot loader thought that all modifier keys were being held down due to a bug in the ADB emulation ; this made it present the (ugly, PC BIOS-like) partition choice screen every time.

When changing the screen depth, there are two hardware components that need to be notified: the video controller and the digital-to-analog converter. DingusPPC had been accidentally relying on the order that Mac OS sent these notifications in; BeOS happened to make the opposite choice and would end up with a corrupted display.

Early versions of BeOS did video memory updates in little-endian mode 1 ; DingusPPC was missing support for that hardware capability.

Later versions of BeOS could mount HFS partitions, but they were having trouble with the volumes that I generated via the machfs Python library. It turned out that BeOS was (correctly) stricter than Mac OS about how some data structures should be populated.

And so on – most of the commits that I upstreamed to DingusPPC over the past month were in a quest for better BeOS compatibility.

SheepShaver , a Power Macintosh emulator that is still around today (and that Infinite Mac also embeds ), originated on BeOS. Mostly for the fun of another layer of inception/emulation, I wanted to make sure that it worked too. As it turned out, it also required a compatibility fix – it relied on an edge case of how the ROM is mapped to physical memory addresses that DingusPPC did not accurately model.

There is a pattern to most of these bug fixes: DingusPPC (and Infinite Mac) have been mostly focused on running Mac OS, and thus accidentally became dependent on its quirks or implementation choices. Adding an independently developed operating system to the mix exercised new paths, and ended up improving the accuracy of the emulated hardware. To be clear, DingusPPC was pretty close out of the box; kudos to its maintainers . I believe that, with this work, it’s the only emulator 2 that can run PowerPC versions of BeOS. I’m also hopeful that this will help with bringing up alternate operating systems like MkLinux (which I also have memories of) and Rhapsody .

On the Infinite Mac side, there were obvious changes like a “BeOS” appearance for my custom controls and collecting software for the library. I also…

items.title: HP Poly VoIP vulnerability sets the stage for executive voice deepfakes
items.content:
HP has released patches for a critical buffer overflow vulnerability in multiple IP-enabled conference phones from its Poly Voice line. The flaw allows unauthenticated attackers to obtain root privileges on the underlying operating system, potentially enabling them to execute other attacks such as eavesdropping on conversations and recording voice data for AI-enabled impersonation attacks.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-0826 , was discovered by researchers from security firm Rapid7 and resides in the code that parses Session Description Protocol (SDP) attributes when the Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE) feature is enabled.

ICE enables VoIP devices to establish peer-to-peer connections using the shortest available network path. The feature is not enabled by default on HP Poly devices, and the company advises administrators to disable it if it’s not needed.

The flaw, rated 9.2 on the CVSS severity scale, affects all phones from the HP Poly VVX series, as well as the Trio 8300, 8500, and 8800 IP conference devices. HP has fixed the flaw in its Poly Unified Communications Software (UCS) versions 6.4.8 for the VVX devices, 8.1.7 for the Trio 8300, and 7.2.8 for Trio 8500 and 8800.

An exploit module targeting this vulnerability has already been developed and released for the widely used Metasploit penetration testing framework that’s maintained by Rapid7.

The exploit executes code as root on an affected device with ICE enabled by sending a SIP INVITE request with a specially crafted candidate attribute. This attribute normally contains a transport address that can be used for connectivity checks and is part of the ICE RFC8839 standard.

The buffer overflow bug is located in a helper function called ParseICECandidate in the polyapp binary that processes such requests on the device.

“The start of the function contains a call to memcpy , which will copy the incoming string line being processed into a 256 byte stack buffer,” Stephen Fewer, senior principal security researcher at Rapid7, said in a blog post . “No length check is performed to ensure the incoming string length is less than 256 bytes. Therefore by providing a candidate attribute whose length is greater than 256 bytes, a stack-based buffer overflow will occur.”

Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR), a kernel feature that randomizes memory addresses to defeat buffer overflow exploits, is enabled on the device. However, the protection is not operating correctly on the HP Poly devices because it does not randomize the load addresses of .so (Shared Object) libraries.

These libraries, such as libc , are loaded by other processes, including the polyapp process, and because their memory addresses never change, they can be leveraged to bypass ASLR and execute the attacker’s payload.

“We create a ROP chain that will execute an arbitrary OS command via the system standard C library function,” Fewer said. “The accompanying Metasploit exploit modules source code details the entire ROP chain.”

Attackers have increasingly targeted embedded devices inside enterprise networks in recent years because unlike laptops, workstations, and servers, these devices are not monitored by endpoint detection and response (EDR) products. As such, they provide perfect footholds inside corporate environments that allow attackers to remain undetected for long periods of time and attack other systems.

In the age of AI these devices become even more relevant for attackers, going beyond corporate espionage by recording conversations or internal network pivoting.

“Attackers no longer need massive datasets to make use of synthetic speech tooling,” Douglas McKee, Rapid7’s director of vulnerability intelligence, said in a blog post . “In many cases, they just need clean source audio of the right person saying enough words in enough contexts. That has made executive voice data, call recordings, and live conversation capture far more valuable than many organizations seem prepared…

items.title: AI-driven layoffs are creating a new class of boomerang employees—companies are realizing they 'pulled the plug too quickly'
items.content:
AI-driven layoffs dominated the headlines this year.

Employers cited AI as the primary reason for almost 40% of the job cuts announced in May 2026, according to a report from outplacement firm Challenger, Gray & Christmas.

But new research shows that some employers may be rethinking those job cuts and reversing course in a trend experts call "AI rebounding."

In a survey of more than 1,000 U.S. workers, nearly 1 in 5 respondents say that they have been laid off or replaced by AI and then asked to return, according to a recent report from SHL, a talent acquisition and talent management company. The survey, which SHL commissioned from market research firm Propeller Insights, also polled over 1,000 U.K. workers. It was conducted between June and July 2026 and had a margin of error of 5%.

These findings indicate that companies are realizing they "pulled the plug too quickly" on their human employees, according to Lucy Beaumont, global senior vice president of product and design at SHL.

Several large employers like Ford and Amazon have reversed course after enacting AI-related layoffs in the past year. A March report by Orgvue found that 32% of organizations that let workers go due to AI have had to rehire staff.

It's a mistake for companies to approach AI implementation as if it were any other software rollout, says Joseph Fuller, professor of management practice at Harvard Business School.

From a company's perspective, "in order to spend money on a new technology, we have to find some savings in the budget, and the way we've done that with previous technology deployments is by laying people off."

But AI is most useful when it's linked with a human worker's "contextual intelligence," i.e. their background knowledge and understanding of an issue, he says: "The more you know about important processes, the more value you can extract from the AI."

AI can't fully replace "people that know the business, that know their customers, that have judgment, that can bring empathy, that have that human connection," Beaumont says.

Most workers are open to returning after a layoff: only 6.6% of U.S. workers say they would refuse to come back under any circumstances, according to the SHL study.

But those who do return are "going to be a lot more demanding of what they expect from an employer," Beaumont says.

According to SHL's research, almost half of surveyed U.S. workers would require a significant pay increase to return to their roles, and 43% would want "written guarantees" of job security. A similar number, 40%, would require "full transparency" regarding how AI would be used in their role before they'd rejoin the company. And 30% of workers say that an apology or acknowledgment from leadership is a key condition of their return.

Above all, employees are looking for reassurance, Beaumont says: "How do I know that this isn't going to happen again?"

Even when workers do return, employers need to understand that company morale is going to take a hit, according to Beaumont. Being laid off "fundamentally changes" the psychological contract between employer and employee, she says, and being rehired isn't enough to repair that relationship.

"You've really broken the trust with those people," Beaumont says.

As a result, returning workers are unlikely to have the same levels of "productivity and engagement" as they did before a layoff, she says. "Culture is so difficult to change, and once you've impacted it negatively, it's so difficult to recover from."

To stay relevant in the job market, employees are prioritizing skill development, Beaumont says: U.S. survey respondents say that they're teaching themselves how to use AI tools (44%), developing industry-specific skills that can't be easily replicated by AI (42.6%), working on interpersonal and leadership skills (40%) and honing creative and strategic thinking (38%).
